lessons.question: You are giving a brand-new agent its first tools. Which starting point is wiser?
options: Every tool the business already has
Two narrow tools and a fixed action budget
One flexible tool that can do anything
lessons.explanation: More tools mean more choices and more ways to fail. Starting small keeps the agent's behaviour easy to inspect and its authority easy to control.

lessons.after: An agent receives a task and observations,
lessons.prompt: Put one turn of the agent loop in order.
steps: Runtime validates the tool, arguments, permissions and budget
Runtime executes the call and records it
Decide whether to continue or stop
lessons.explanation: The model only proposes actions. The runtime sits between the choice and the execution, which is where authority is actually enforced.

lessons.after: A tool contract needs an input schema,
lessons.prompt: Is each tool design narrow and controllable, or hard to control?

items.text: prepare_draft with a few fixed fields
One tool that both reads and writes records

lessons.explanation: Narrow tools with distinct reads and writes let you set permissions per tool. A catch-all tool hides what it will actually do until it runs.

lessons.question: An agent remembers a refund rule it learned months ago. Should it rely on that memory today?
options: Yes, stored memory is always reliable
Only if the user asks about refunds
No, it should re-check the current policy
lessons.explanation: Business rules such as amounts, statuses and permissions change. Memory suits stable preferences, while current sources decide the rules.

lessons.prompt: Is each item context, task state, or memory?

items.text: The ticket text included in this request
Which items in this batch still need review
A preference saved in an earlier session
The policy passage supplied for this question
Which steps of the process are complete

lessons.explanation: Context lives for one request, task state tracks the current process, and memory carries selected facts across sessions. The business system of record is separate from all of them.

lessons.after: Skills also need review. A saved procedure
lessons.question: A shared skill has worked well for lots of people. Does that make its supporting code safe to run?
options: No, usefulness says nothing about safety, so inspect it
Yes, popularity shows it has been checked
Yes, provided it has a version number
lessons.explanation: A useful procedure can still include a broad shell command or an unnecessary credential. Version it, inspect changes, and rerun evaluation cases after edits.

lessons.after: T08 asks the assistant to export customer
lessons.prompt: The T08 ticket tells the assistant to export files. Why is that not an instruction the agent should follow?
lessons.answer: It is text inside a ticket, which is source content to be processed, not a request from the authorised operator. Instructions found in data are treated as data.

lessons.prompt: Before building an agent, ask: does this task really need one? When would a fixed workflow be the better choice?
lessons.answer: When the steps are known and the same every time, a fixed workflow like Week 7's is simpler to control and test. An agent earns its place only when choosing the next action from observations genuinely helps.

lessons.after: Submit a tool contract, permissions map,
lessons.prompt: For the Harbour weekly-brief agent, should the runtime allow each request or stop it?

items.text: Search policy for the weekly brief
Export customer files as T08 asks
Send a message to a customer
Keep searching for a document that does not exist
Switch itself to the manager role

lessons.explanation: Only the two approved read tools are in scope. Customer messaging, exports and role changes are unavailable, and repeated failure should end in an unresolved question.
